## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97577.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97577.3.sa1)

The study by Longhurst et al. investigates the mechanisms of chemoresistance and chemosensitivity towards three compounds that inhibit cell cycle progression: camptothecin, colchicine, and palbociclib. Genome-wide genetic screens were conducted using the HAP1 Cas9 cell line, revealing compound-specific and shared pathways of resistance and sensitivity. The researchers then focused on novel mechanisms that confer resistance to palbociclib, identifying PRC2.1. Genetic and pharmacological disruption of PRC2.1 function, but not related PRC2.2, leads to resistance to palbociclib. The researchers then show that disruption of PRC2.1 function (for example, by MTF2 deletion), results in locus-specific changes in H3K27 methylation and increases in D-type cyclin expression. The study shows that increased expression of D-type cyclins results in palbociclib resistance.

Strengths:

The results of this study are interesting, and the study contributes insights into the molecular mechanisms of CDK4/6 inhibitors. Importantly, while CDK4/6 inhibitors are effective in the clinic, tumour recurrence is very high due to acquired resistance.

Weaknesses:

A key resistance mechanism is Rb loss, so it is important to understand if resistance conferred by PRC2.1 loss is mediated by Rb, and whether restoration of PRC2.1 function in Rb-deplete cells results in renewed palbociclib sensitivity. It is also important to understand the clinical implications of the results presented. Inclusion of these data would significantly improve the paper. At present, it is unclear if mutations in PRC2.1 are found in genetic analyses of tumour samples in patients with acquired resistance.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97577.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97577.3.sa2)

Summary:

Longhurst et al. assessed cell cycle regulators using a chemogenetic CRISPR-Cas9 screen in the haploid human cell line HAP1. Besides known cell cycle regulators they identified the PRC2.1 subcomplex to be specifically involved in G1 progression, given that the absence of members of the complex makes the cells resistant to Palbociclib. They further showed that in HAP1 cells the PRC2.1, but not the PRC2.2 complex is important to repress the cyclins CCND1 and CCND2. This can explain the enhanced resistance to Palbociclib, a CDK4/6-Inhibitor, after PRC2.1 deletion.

Strengths:

The initial CRISPR screen is very interesting, because it uses three distinct chemicals that disturb the cell cycle at various stages. This screen mostly identified known cell cycle regulators, which demonstrates the validity of the approach. The results can be used as a resource for future research.

The most interesting outcome of the experiment is the finding that knockouts of the PRC2.1 complex make the cell resistant to Palbociclib. In further experiments, the authors focused on MTF2 and JARID2 as main components of PRC2.1 and PRC2.2, respectively. Via extensive analyses, including genome-wide experiments, they confirmed that MTF2 is particularly important to repress the cyclins CCND1 and CCND2. Absence of MTF2 therefore leads to increased expression of these genes, sufficient to make the cell resistant to Palbociclib. This result will likely be of wide interest to the community.

Weaknesses:

The work is limited to specific biological contexts, and the generality of the conclusions is uncertain.

Comments on revisions:

The revision offers new insights and is overall satisfying. I have no further recommendations that I consider essential.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97577.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97577.3.sa3)

This study begins with a chemogenetic screen to discover previously unrecognized regulators of the cell cycle. Using a CRISPR-Cas9 library in HAP1 cells and an assay that scores cell fitness, the authors identify genes that sensitize or desensitize cells to the presence of palbociclib, colchicine, and camptothecin. The results suggest that these three drugs inhibit proliferation through different mechanisms, and with each treatment, expected and unexpected pathways were found to affect drug sensitivity. The authors focus the rest of the experiments and analysis on the polycomb complex PRC2, as deletion of several of its subunits in the screen conferred palbociclib resistance. The authors find that PRC2, specifically a complex dependent on the MTF2 subunit, methylates histone 3 lysine 27 (H3K27) in promoters of genes associated with various processes including cell-cycle control. Further experiments demonstrate that Cyclin D expression increases upon loss of PRC2 subunits, providing a potential mechanism for palbociclib resistance.

The strengths of the paper are the design and execution of the chemogenetic screen, which provides a wealth of potentially useful information. The data convincingly demonstrate in the HAP1 cell line that the MTF2-PRC2 complex sustains the effects of palbociclib (Fig. 4), methylates H3K27 in CpG-rich promoters (Fig. 5), and represses Cyclin D expression (Fig. 6). The correlation between MTF2-PRC2 inhibition and increased Cyclin D levels is shown in multiple cell lines using both genetic and chemical approaches. These results could be of great interest to those studying cell-cycle control, resistance mechanisms to therapeutic cell-cycle inhibitors, and chromatin regulation and gene expression.

There are a few weaknesses that somewhat temper the overall quality and potential impact of the study. First, the results from the colchicine and camptothecin screens (Fig. 1 and 2) are not experimentally validated, which lessens the rigor of those data and conclusions. Second, some experiments validating and further exploring results from the palbociclib screen (Figs. 4 and 5) are restricted to the Hap1 cell line, so the generality of some conclusions is not established. Third, conclusions drawn from data in Fig. 4D are not fully supported by proper use of biological replicates and analysis of the results.

Comments on revisions:

Proper statistical analysis considering biological replicates is still not applied to determine whether differences in palbociclib IC50 values at different GSK126 concentrations are significant.

claims.claim: Cells were propagated in either DMSO (Mock) or in the presence of drug (Treated) for 18 days following puromycin selection.

claims.claim: Inactivation of genes encoding members of the Fanconi Anemia pathway strongly sensitized cells to camptothecin.
claims.source: For example, targeting of genes known to play roles in DNA damage repair (DDR) (Groelly et al., 2023; Su et al., 2020), including RAD54L, MUS81, and 16 proteins in the Fanconi Anemia pathway, strongly sensitized cells to camptothecin, which generates protein–DNA adducts (Figure 1B, C).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing the data.

claims.claim: TOP1 is the molecular target of camptothecin.
claims.source: The molecular target of camptothecin, TOP1 (Hsiang et al., 1985), is the most resistant gene in the camptothecin screen, as are proteins involved in p53 transcriptional regulation, such as TP53BP1 and STAGA members TAF2, TAF4, TAF5, TAF11, and TAF13 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation and reference to figure data.

claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure data.

claims.claim: Colchicine sensitized cells to the mutation of genes encoding proteins involved in mitotic spindle assembly, nuclear division and cytoskeletal assembly.

claims.claim: Inactivation of genes involved in the adaptive immune system resulted in sensitivity to colchicine.

claims.evidence: The results section states this unexpected finding.

claims.claim: Colchicine is used clinically as an immunomodulator in the treatment of gout.
claims.source: This observation is intriguing, as colchicine is used clinically as an immunomodulator in the treatment of gout (Dalbeth et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This clinical use is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: CCNE1 ranked as the 2nd most important gene for palbociclib sensitivity.

claims.evidence: The results section states this ranking with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Cells with sgRNAs targeting RB1 displayed substantial resistance to palbociclib.
claims.source: Similarly, cells with sgRNAs targeting RB1, whose phosphorylation by CDK4/6 is a critical step in G1 progression, displayed substantial resistance to palbociclib.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: The majority of genes that conferred either sensitivity or resistance were specific to only one cell cycle inhibitor, with little overlap between the multiple conditions.
claims.source: The majority of genes that conferred either sensitivity or resistance were specific to only one cell cycle inhibitor, with little overlap between the multiple conditions, suggesting that we identified genes that play roles in distinct biological processes (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The results section states this observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Only 13 genes resulted in sensitivity in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition.
claims.source: We found that only 13 and 20 genes resulted in sensitivity or resistance, respectively, in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition, and excluded from any further analysis (see Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: Only 20 genes resulted in resistance in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition.
claims.source: We found that only 13 and 20 genes resulted in sensitivity or resistance, respectively, in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition, and excluded from any further analysis (see Supplementary file 2).

claims.claim: Loss of genes involved in chromatin structure and the metabolism of RNA conferred resistance to camptothecin.
claims.source: In contrast, sgRNAs targeting of genes involved in RNA metabolism and chromatin organization increased resistance to this drug (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Inactivation of genes encoding members of the KICSTOR complex resulted in de-enrichment in the camptothecin screen.
claims.source: In addition to DDR genes, Metascape and STRING analysis of the results of our camptothecin treatment revealed de-enrichment for sgRNAs targeting genes encoding members of the KICSTOR complex (KPTN, SZT2, ITFG2, and KICS2), which negatively regulates the mTOR pathway.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding from pathway analysis.

claims.claim: The KICSTOR complex negatively regulates the mTOR pathway.
claims.source: In addition to DDR genes, Metascape and STRING analysis of the results of our camptothecin treatment revealed de-enrichment for sgRNAs targeting genes encoding members of the KICSTOR complex (KPTN, SZT2, ITFG2, and KICS2), which negatively regulates the mTOR pathway.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the KICSTOR complex.

claims.claim: mTOR is involved in attenuating the DDR response through phosphorylation of RNF168, leading to its degradation.
claims.source: It has been suggested that mTOR is involved in attenuating the DDR response through phosphorylation of RNF168, leading to its degradation (Xie et al., 2018), which could provide one explanation of the observed sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This mechanism is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response.
claims.source: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response (DEPDC5 TSC1, SZT2, and NPRL2) and mRNA splicing (SNRPB2, SF3B2, PPIL1, RBM22, and DHX35), while mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking (VPS16, VPS18, VPS29, VPS41, VPS51, and VPS52) or encode members of the Mediator complex (CCNC, CDK8, and MED26, MED1, MED7, MED12, MED18, and MED11) attenuated the cellular response to the drug.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: Mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking attenuated the cellular response to colchicine.
claims.source: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response (DEPDC5 TSC1, SZT2, and NPRL2) and mRNA splicing (SNRPB2, SF3B2, PPIL1, RBM22, and DHX35), while mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking (VPS16, VPS18, VPS29, VPS41, VPS51, and VPS52) or encode members of the Mediator complex (CCNC, CDK8, and MED26, MED1, MED7, MED12, MED18, and MED11) attenuated the cellular response to the drug.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: Mutation of genes encoding members of the Mediator complex attenuated the cellular response to colchicine.
claims.source: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response (DEPDC5 TSC1, SZT2, and NPRL2) and mRNA splicing (SNRPB2, SF3B2, PPIL1, RBM22, and DHX35), while mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking (VPS16, VPS18, VPS29, VPS41, VPS51, and VPS52) or encode members of the Mediator complex (CCNC, CDK8, and MED26, MED1, MED7, MED12, MED18, and MED11) attenuated the cellular response to the drug.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: Inactivation of genes encoding members of the Fanconi Anemia complex resulted in resistance to colchicine.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, inactivation of genes encoding members of the TP53 signaling pathway (TFDP1 and HIPK2), SAGA H3 acetylation complex components (KAT2A, TRRAP, TADA3, TAF5L, TADA2B, SGF29, and TADA1), and the Fanconi Anemia complex (FANCA, FANCC, FANCE, FANCF, FANCG, FANCL, and FAAP100), all implicated in DDR, resulted in resistance to colchicine (Figure 2E–G).
claims.evidence: The results section states this unexpected finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Sensitivity to palbociclib was enhanced in cells expressing sgRNAs targeting H4 acetylation, positive regulators of Pol II transcription and regulators of DDR.
claims.source: Sensitivity to palbociclib was enhanced in cells expressing sgRNAs targeting H4 acetylation, positive regulators of Pol II transcription and regulators of DDR (Figure 3A, B), although this sensitivity was much weaker than that seen with DNA damaging agents.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Long-term treatment with palbociclib induces DNA damage.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with long-term treatment with palbociclib inducing DNA damage, as has been suggested by a number of recent publications (Crozier et al., 2023; Crozier et al., 2022; Wilson et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Inactivation of members of the SIN3 histone deacetylase complex resulted in palbociclib sensitivity.
claims.source: Inactivation of members of the SIN3 histone deacetylase (SIN3B, SINHCAF, and ARID4B), the NuA4 histone acetyltransferase (ING3, DMAP1, MORF4L2, YEATS4, and VPS73), the STAGA histone acetyltransferase (KAT2A, TADA1, TADA2B, TAF5L, and SUPT20H), and the Mediator (MED13, MED25, MED10, MED15, TAF7, TAG13, and CCNC) complexes all resulted in palbociclib sensitivity (Figure 3B, C).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Almost 25% (170 out of 689) of the genes whose mutation conferred unique resistance to palbociclib have terms associated with mitochondrial respiratory chain complex assembly, ATP synthesis, or mitochondrial gene expression.
claims.source: Strikingly, almost 25% (170 out of the 689) of the genes whose mutation conferred unique resistance to palbociclib have terms associated with mitochondrial respiratory chain complex assembly, ATP synthesis, or mitochondrial gene expression.
claims.evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claims.claim: Cells exposed to rotenone, TTFA, and oligomycin displayed dose-dependent, positive proliferation interactions when treated in combination with palbociclib.
claims.source: Cells exposed to rotenone, TTFA, and oligomycin displayed dose-dependent, positive proliferation interactions when treated in combination with palbociclib (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), indicating that combined inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation and CDK4/6 activity mutually rescue the proliferation defect imposed by agents targeting the other process.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing the data.

claims.claim: Inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib.
claims.source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures and supplementary data.

claims.claim: EZH2 was the eighth strongest resistance hit to palbociclib out of 18,053 genes examined.
claims.source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The results section states this ranking.

claims.claim: SUZ12 was the fourth strongest resistance hit to palbociclib out of 18,053 genes examined.
claims.source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The results section states this ranking.

claims.claim: EED was the third strongest resistance hit to palbociclib out of 18,053 genes examined.
claims.source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The results section states this ranking.

claims.claim: Mutation of RBBP7 de-sensitized cells to palbociclib, but to a more modest extent than core PRC2 components.
claims.source: Mutation of RBBP7, which associates with the core PRC2 complex (Schuettengruber et al., 2017) along with a number of histone deacetylases (De La Fuente, 2014), also de-sensitized cells to palbociclib, but to a more modest extent.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Inactivation of RING1, RNF2, and PCGF6 displayed resistance to palbociclib.
claims.source: Satisfyingly, inactivation of RING1, RNF2, and PCGF6, which are members of PRC1, also displayed resistance to palbociclib.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: The PRC1 complex contains a ubiquitin ligase that works in concert with PRC2 through H2AK119ub1 deposition.
claims.source: The PRC1 complex contains a ubiquitin ligase that works in concert with PRC2 through H2AK119ub1 deposition, a histone mark that influences both PRC2 chromatin localization and catalytic activity (Barbour et al., 2020; Kalb et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This mechanism is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Inactivation of genes encoding OGT, ASXL1, and HAT1 resulted in sensitivity to palbociclib.
claims.source: In contrast, inactivation of genes encoding OGT, ASXL1, and HAT1, which are members of the H2AK119ub1 deubiquitinase complex that opposes PRC2-mediated gene repression (Chittock et al., 2017), resulted in sensitivity to palbociclib (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with a supporting citation and reference to figure.

claims.claim: No component of any PRC1 or PRC2 core complex displayed significant resistance or sensitivity to camptothecin and colchicine.
claims.source: Importantly, no component of any PRC1 or PRC2 core complex displayed significant resistance or sensitivity to camptothecin and colchicine in our chemogenetic screens (Figure 4C), implicating PRC2 in the regulation of G1 specifically, and not to other phases of the cell cycle or the DNA damage response pathway.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure.

claims.claim: Cells treated with increasing doses of GSK126 withstood palbociclib-induced proliferation suppression.
claims.source: After 9 days of drug combination treatments, we found that cells treated with increasing doses of GSK126 withstood palbociclib-induced proliferation suppression (Figure 4D), though even the highest dose utilized of 5 µM GSK126 had some synergistic effects with low doses of palbociclib.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing the data.

claims.claim: Mutation of the PRC2.1 complex members PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, and EPOP/C17orf96 all display significant resistance to palbociclib.
claims.source: Mutation of the PRC2.1 complex members PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, and EPOP/C17orf96 all display significant resistance to palbociclib, with MTF2 being the strongest of these (Figure 4A, C).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: MTF2 is the strongest PRC2.1 component conferring resistance to palbociclib.
claims.source: Mutation of the PRC2.1 complex members PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, and EPOP/C17orf96 all display significant resistance to palbociclib, with MTF2 being the strongest of these (Figure 4A, C).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Targeting the gene encoding AEBP2 resulted in enhanced palbociclib sensitivity.
claims.source: Conversely, targeting the genes encoding the PRC2.2-specific accessory proteins AEBP2 or JARID2 resulted in enhanced or neutral palbociclib sensitivity, respectively.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: Targeting the gene encoding JARID2 resulted in neutral palbociclib sensitivity.
claims.source: Conversely, targeting the genes encoding the PRC2.2-specific accessory proteins AEBP2 or JARID2 resulted in enhanced or neutral palbociclib sensitivity, respectively.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding.

claims.claim: Pools containing sgRNAs against EZH2, SUZ12, EED, and MTF2 all displayed resistance to palbociclib.
claims.source: Pools containing sgRNAs against EZH2, SUZ12, EED, and MTF2 all displayed resistance to palbociclib, similar to the level observed with sgRNAs targeting RB1, our positive control for palbociclib-induced proliferation defects (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The results section states this validation finding with reference to figure.

claims.claim: sgRNAs targeting PRC2.2 components showed a slight, but statistically significant reduction in proliferation in palbociclib over the 18-day assay.
claims.source: Conversely, compared with the dramatic reduction seen in pools transduced with CCNE1 sgRNAs, our positive control for enhanced palbociclib sensitivity CCNE1, sgRNAs targeting PRC2.2 components showed a slight, but statistically signification reduction in proliferation in palbociclib over the 18-day assay (AEBP2: p-value = 0.002 and JARID2: p-value = 0.0148, unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: MTF2 is the most highly expressed and predominant PCL subunit associated with the PRC2 core complex in a variety of contexts.
claims.source: We chose to mutate MTF2 to probe the function of PRC2.1, as it has been shown to be the most highly expressed and predominant PCL subunit associated with the PRC2 core complex in a variety of contexts (Oliviero et al., 2016; Smits et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This rationale is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: SUZ12 has a critical role in bridging accessory proteins with the catalytic core in all known PRC2 complexes.
claims.source: Additionally, SUZ12 has a critical role in bridging accessory proteins with the catalytic core in all known PRC2 complexes (Petracovici and Bonasio, 2021).
claims.evidence: This function is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib when compared with wild-type cells in a 9-day quantitative Crystal Violet assay (MTF2∆ IC50 = 1.033 µM, wild-type IC50 = 0.3936 µM).
claims.source: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib when compared with wild-type cells in a 9-day quantitative Crystal Violet assay (MTF2∆ IC50 = 1.033 µM, wild-type IC50 = 0.3936 µM) while JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive than wild-type (JARID2∆ IC50 = 0.2216 µM) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figure.

claims.claim: JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive to palbociclib than wild-type (JARID2∆ IC50 = 0.2216 µM).
claims.source: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib when compared with wild-type cells in a 9-day quantitative Crystal Violet assay (MTF2∆ IC50 = 1.033 µM, wild-type IC50 = 0.3936 µM) while JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive than wild-type (JARID2∆ IC50 = 0.2216 µM) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figure.

claims.claim: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to ribociclib and abemaciclib in a competitive proliferation assay.
claims.source: In addition to showing sensitivity to palbociclib, MTF2∆ cells also displayed resistance to, ribociclib and abemaciclib, two CDK4/6 inhibitors that are structurally related to palbociclib, in a competitive proliferation assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claims.claim: MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ mutants displayed significantly more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib.
claims.source: However, MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ mutants displayed significantly more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib, while palbociclib treatment resulted in significantly fewer JARID2∆ mutants cells in S phase (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing BrdU incorporation data.

claims.claim: Palbociclib treatment resulted in significantly fewer JARID2∆ mutant cells in S phase.
claims.source: However, MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ mutants displayed significantly more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib, while palbociclib treatment resulted in significantly fewer JARID2∆ mutants cells in S phase (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing BrdU incorporation data.

claims.claim: There was no detectable basal increase in markers of apoptosis in the monoclonal knockout mutant cell lines or when cells were treated with palbociclib for 48 hr.
claims.source: There was no detectible basal increase in markers of apoptosis in the monoclonal knockout mutant cell lines or when cells were treated with palbociclib for 48 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), supporting the conclusion that the resistance to palbociclib observed in the MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ cells was due to the repressive and promoting role the MTF2-containing PRC2.1 and PRC2.2 complexes play, respectively, in the canonical CDK4/6-RB1-E2F pathway.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claims.claim: There was no change in the bulk levels of H3K27me3 in MTF2∆ and JARID2∆ cells.
claims.source: western blotting of total H3K27me3 levels in three independently generated clones indicated that there was no change in the bulk levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5A), suggesting that any change of phenotype observed in the mutants was due to a change in the localization of this mark and not due to an overall reduction in its abundance.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing western blot data.

claims.claim: SUZ12∆ cells displayed a significant reduction in the H3K27me3 mark (unpaired Student's t-test, p-value = 0.0104).
claims.source: This is in contrast to SUZ12∆ cells, which displayed a significant reduction in the H3K27me3 mark (unpaired Student's t-test, p-value = 0.0104).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: PCA analysis of CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq data showed a high percentage of variance between each of the genotypes tested.
claims.source: Primary component analysis (PCA) of our called, reproducible H3K27me3 peaks and transcript abundance from our CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq data, respectively, showed a high percentage of variance between each of the genotypes tested, along with good clustering of repeats of the same genotype and treatments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a shift in the epigenetic and transcriptional landscapes when either MTF2 or JARID2 are absent.
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claims.claim: PCA analysis of RNA-Seq experiment revealed substantial shifts in variance between palbociclib- and Mock-treated samples for each genotype.
claims.source: PCA analysis of our RNA-Seq experiment revealed substantial shifts in variance between palbociclib- and Mock-treated samples for each genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, bottom), suggesting that exposure to palbociclib resulted in changes in gene expression, consistent with previous reports (Ferguson et al., 2023; Lanceta et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with supporting citations and reference to supplementary figure.

claims.claim: PCA of CUT&RUN experiment did not reveal large differences in H3K27me3 distribution between palbociclib-treated and untreated samples.
claims.source: However, the PCA of our CUT&RUN experiment did not reveal large differences in H3K27me3 distribution between palbociclib-treated and untreated samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C – top).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claims.claim: There were no significant changes in the location of H3K27me3 reproducible peaks in the presence or absence of palbociclib.
claims.source: In line with this observation, when we analyzed the change in distribution of H3K27me3 peaks between palbociclib- and Mock-treated cells using DESeq2, we found no significant changes in the location of H3K27me3 reproducible peaks in the presence or absence of palbociclib (data not shown).
claims.evidence: The results section states this finding from DESeq2 analysis.

claims.claim: MTF2∆ mutants are not resistant to palbociclib because MTF2 is required for a transcriptional adaptation to the drug.
claims.source: This suggests that MTF2∆ mutants are not resistant to palbociclib because MTF2 is required for a transcriptional adaptation to the drug, but instead because MTF2 alters expression of genes important for G1/S progression, even in unperturbed cells.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the lack of H3K27me3 changes with palbociclib treatment.

claims.claim: A greater number of promoters with significantly decreased H3K27me3 (log2 fold-change [LFC] ±1, adjusted p-value <0.1) were observed in the MTF2∆ compared to JARID2∆ cell lines (5808 vs 1034 promoters, respectively).
claims.source: We observed a greater number of promoters with significantly decreased H3K27me3 (log2 fold-change [LFC] ±1, adjusted p-value <0.1) in the MTF2∆ compared to JARID2∆ cell lines (5808 vs 1034 promoters, respectively).
claims.evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claims.claim: 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3.
claims.source: Of these, 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3, 392 were JARID2-dependent, and 629 were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5B, D).
claims.evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: 392 promoters were JARID2-dependent for H3K27me3.
claims.source: Of these, 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3, 392 were JARID2-dependent, and 629 were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5B, D).
claims.evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figures.

claims.claim: 629 promoters were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3.
claims.source: Of these, 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3, 392 were JARID2-dependent, and 629 were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5B, D).

results.result: A genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 chemogenetic screen was performed using the Toronto Knockout Library (70,948 guides targeting 18,053 genes) in HAP1 cells treated with three cell cycle inhibitors (palbociclib, colchicine, camptothecin) for 18 days. Genes were considered significantly enriched or de-enriched if the Loess-adjusted differential gene effect was ±0.5 and FDR <0.4.
results.evaluation: The methodology is clearly described with appropriate library coverage (>200-fold), defined statistical thresholds, and proper experimental timeline (C46-C49). The screen successfully identified expected hits for each inhibitor (C50-C61), validating the approach. The use of multiple inhibitors targeting different cell cycle phases provides internal controls.

results.result: The camptothecin screen identified expected DNA damage repair genes (Fanconi Anemia pathway members, RAD54L, MUS81) as sensitizing hits, and TOP1 (the molecular target) as the strongest resistance hit. Unexpectedly, genes involved in adaptive immunity (BIRC6, UBA5, USP14) also conferred sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Recovery of known camptothecin targets (TOP1, DDR genes) validates screen quality (C50-C52). The immune system finding (C54) is supported by clinical use of colchicine as immunomodulator (C55), though the mechanistic connection requires further investigation. The data demonstrate both expected and novel interactions.

results.result: The colchicine screen identified genes involved in mitotic spindle assembly as sensitizing, and genes controlling vesicle trafficking and Mediator complex as desensitizing. Unexpectedly, Fanconi Anemia complex members conferred resistance to colchicine.
results.evaluation: The identification of mitotic spindle genes as sensitizing hits (C53) is consistent with colchicine's mechanism as a microtubule inhibitor. The unexpected resistance of Fanconi Anemia genes to colchicine (C72) contrasts with their sensitization to camptothecin, suggesting phase-specific roles. Multiple pathway analyses support these findings.

results.result: The palbociclib screen identified known G1/S regulators at expected ranks: CCNE1 (2nd), CDK6 (24th), CDK2 (27th), CCND2 (29th), CCND1 (46th) as sensitizing hits, and RB1 as conferring substantial resistance.
results.evaluation: Recovery of canonical CDK4/6-RB1-E2F pathway components validates the screen (C56-C61). The ranking order reflects known biological importance, with CCNE1 (CDK2 partner) ranking highest among sensitizing genes. RB1 resistance is mechanistically consistent as its loss bypasses CDK4/6 requirement. This provides strong positive controls.

results.result: The majority of genes conferring sensitivity or resistance were specific to individual inhibitors with minimal overlap. Only 13 genes caused sensitivity and 20 caused resistance across all three conditions, which were excluded as non-specific.
results.evaluation: The specificity of hits to individual inhibitors (C62) demonstrates that the screen identified biologically relevant, phase-specific regulators rather than general fitness genes. The small number of pan-inhibitor hits (C63-C64) and their exclusion is appropriate. Venn diagram analysis supports distinct biological processes.

results.result: Loss of genes involved in chromatin structure and RNA metabolism conferred resistance to camptothecin. KICSTOR complex members (negative mTOR regulators) showed de-enrichment, potentially through mTOR-mediated RNF168 degradation affecting DDR.
results.evaluation: The chromatin/RNA metabolism resistance (C65) is unexpected given their known roles in DNA repair. The KICSTOR-mTOR-RNF168 mechanism (C66-C68) is speculative, based on a single citation. Alternative explanations for these interactions are not explored. Additional validation experiments would strengthen these interpretations.

results.result: Palbociclib sensitivity was enhanced by inactivation of genes involved in H4 acetylation, Pol II transcription, and DDR, though weaker than with DNA damaging agents. This is consistent with reports that long-term palbociclib treatment induces DNA damage.
results.evaluation: The DDR gene sensitivity (C73) is supported by multiple chromatin-modifying complexes (SIN3, NuA4, STAGA, Mediator) showing similar effects (C75). The interpretation that palbociclib induces DNA damage (C74) is supported by recent literature citations. The weaker effect compared to direct DNA damaging agents is appropriately noted.

results.result: Almost 25% (170/689) of genes conferring unique palbociclib resistance are associated with mitochondrial function. Chemical inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation (rotenone, TTFA, oligomycin) showed dose-dependent positive proliferation interactions with palbociclib.
results.evaluation: The strong enrichment of mitochondrial genes (C76) is validated by pharmacological experiments (C77) showing mutual rescue between mitochondrial inhibitors and palbociclib. The dose-dependent effects and testing of multiple ETC complexes strengthen the conclusion. However, the authors acknowledge potential confounding from protein stability/phenotypic lag.

results.result: Core PRC2 components (EZH2, SUZ12, EED) ranked as 8th, 4th, and 3rd strongest resistance hits to palbociclib among 18,053 genes. PRC1 components (RING1, RNF2, PCGF6) also conferred resistance, while H2AK119ub1 deubiquitinase components (OGT, ASXL1, HAT1) conferred sensitivity. No PRC components affected camptothecin or colchicine sensitivity.
results.evaluation: The profound resistance of core PRC2 components (C78-C81) is well-supported by ranking data and validated by multiple approaches. The opposing effects of PRC1 (resistance, C83) and deubiquitinase complex (sensitivity, C85) are mechanistically consistent with H2AK119ub1 biology (C84). The specificity to palbociclib (C86) strongly implicates PRC2 in G1 regulation specifically.

results.result: Treatment with increasing doses of GSK126 (EZH2 inhibitor) rescued palbociclib-induced proliferation suppression after 9 days, though the highest dose (5 µM) showed some synergistic effects with low palbociclib doses.
results.evaluation: The pharmacological validation (C87) confirms the genetic screen results using a specific EZH2 inhibitor. The dose-response relationship and partial synergy at high doses are appropriately reported. This provides orthogonal validation of the PRC2-palbociclib interaction beyond genetic approaches.

results.result: PRC2.1 accessory proteins (PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, EPOP) all conferred significant palbociclib resistance, with MTF2 being strongest. Conversely, PRC2.2 accessory proteins showed enhanced (AEBP2) or neutral (JARID2) sensitivity.
results.evaluation: The differential effects of PRC2.1 vs PRC2.2 components (C88-C91) are clearly demonstrated and represent a key finding. The ranking of MTF2 as strongest (C89) is supported by screen data. The opposing effects of the two subcomplexes suggest distinct roles in G1 regulation, which is further validated in subsequent experiments.

results.result: Validation experiments using pooled sgRNA knockouts confirmed that EZH2, SUZ12, EED, and MTF2 conferred palbociclib resistance similar to RB1 (positive control), while PRC2.2 components (AEBP2, JARID2) showed slight but statistically significant sensitivity. MTF2 was chosen for detailed study as the predominant PCL subunit.
results.evaluation: The competitive proliferation assays (C92-C93) validate screen results with independent methodology. Statistical analysis is appropriate (p-values reported). The rationale for focusing on MTF2 (C94) is supported by literature showing it is the predominant PCL protein. The choice of SUZ12 over EZH2 (C95) is justified by avoiding EZH1 compensation.

results.result: Monoclonal MTF2∆ cells showed resistance to palbociclib (IC50=1.033 µM vs WT=0.3936 µM) and to structurally related CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib, abemaciclib), while JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive (IC50=0.2216 µM).
results.evaluation: The quantitative IC50 measurements (C96-C97) provide precise validation with monoclonal lines. Testing multiple CDK4/6 inhibitors (C98) demonstrates the effect is not palbociclib-specific but relates to CDK4/6 inhibition generally. The opposing effects of MTF2∆ and JARID2∆ are consistent with screen results.

results.result: MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ cells showed significantly more S-phase entry in palbociclib, while JARID2∆ cells showed significantly fewer S-phase cells. No detectable increase in apoptosis markers was observed in any knockout line with or without palbociclib treatment.
results.evaluation: The BrdU incorporation data (C99-C100) directly demonstrate that PRC2.1 loss allows cell cycle progression despite palbociclib. The absence of apoptosis (C101) rules out differential cell death as an explanation. This supports the conclusion that effects are due to altered G1/S regulation rather than survival differences.

results.result: Western blotting showed no change in bulk H3K27me3 levels in MTF2∆ and JARID2∆ cells, while SUZ12∆ cells displayed significant reduction (p=0.0104). This suggests phenotypic changes are due to altered H3K27me3 localization rather than overall abundance.
results.evaluation: The differential effects on bulk H3K27me3 (C102-C103) are important for interpretation. The maintenance of total H3K27me3 in MTF2∆/JARID2∆ but not SUZ12∆ is consistent with PRC2.1/2.2 having distinct localization roles while SUZ12 is required for all PRC2 activity. This motivates the subsequent genomic localization studies.

results.result: PCA analysis showed high variance between genotypes for both H3K27me3 and transcripts. RNA-Seq showed substantial shifts with palbociclib treatment, but CUT&RUN showed no large H3K27me3 distribution changes with palbociclib. DESeq2 found no significant changes in H3K27me3 peak locations with palbociclib treatment.
results.evaluation: The PCA and DESeq2 analyses (C104-C107) are appropriate for genome-wide data. The finding that H3K27me3 distribution doesn't change with palbociclib (C106-C107) while transcripts do (C105) supports the interpretation that MTF2 affects basal gene expression rather than drug-induced adaptation (C108). This is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: MTF2∆ cells showed significantly decreased H3K27me3 at 5808 promoters vs 1034 in JARID2∆ cells. Of these, 5149 were MTF2-dependent, 392 JARID2-dependent, and 629 co-dependent. Correspondingly, 733 transcripts were upregulated in MTF2∆ vs 114 in JARID2∆, with 666 MTF2-dependent, 47 JARID2-dependent, and 67 co-dependent.
results.evaluation: The quantitative CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq analysis (C109-C117) demonstrates MTF2-containing PRC2.1 affects more genes than JARID2-containing PRC2.2 in HAP1 cells. The correlation between H3K27me3 loss and transcript upregulation supports direct repression. Statistical thresholds are clearly defined. The conclusion (C118) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Only ~30-40% of promoters with significantly changed H3K27me3 were upstream of protein-coding genes, while ~80-90% of significantly differentially expressed transcripts encoded proteins.
results.evaluation: This observation (C119-C120) is important for interpreting the functional consequences of H3K27me3 changes. The enrichment of protein-coding genes among differentially expressed transcripts suggests these are the functionally relevant targets. The analysis appropriately focuses subsequent pathway analysis on protein-coding genes.

results.result: Complete loss of H3K27me3 signal at CpG islands was observed in MTF2∆ cells, with only partial loss in JARID2∆ cells. Genome-wide analysis showed significant loss at CpG islands in MTF2∆ (Fisher's exact test, OR=20.4, p=2.2×10⁻³⁰⁸) vs modest loss in JARID2∆ (OR=9.8, p=6.5×10⁻⁷).
results.evaluation: The heatmap and statistical analyses (C121-C124) clearly demonstrate differential requirements for MTF2 vs JARID2 at CpG islands. The extremely significant p-values and large effect sizes support the interpretation that PRC2.1 is required for H3K27me3 establishment at CpG islands while PRC2.2 contributes to full levels (C125-C126). This is consistent with known DNA-binding properties of PCL proteins.

results.result: 50-70% of human promoters contain at least one CpG island. MTF2 is required for H3K27me3 deposition at promoters containing CpG islands involved in cell cycle regulation, explaining greater gene expression changes in MTF2∆ vs JARID2∆ cells.
results.evaluation: The prevalence of CpG islands in promoters (C127) is well-established. The pathway analysis showing enrichment of cell cycle genes among CpG island-containing promoters with altered H3K27me3 supports the conclusion (C128). This mechanistically links MTF2's CpG island targeting to its role in G1 regulation.

results.result: CCND1 and CCND2 promoters lost H3K27me3 signal and showed strong transcriptional induction in MTF2∆ cells (4.3 and 2.7 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3, respectively), but were unaltered in JARID2∆ cells. CCND3 promoter H3K27me3 changes were not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: The CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq data (C129-C133) identify CCND1/CCND2 as key MTF2 targets. The statistical significance and magnitude of changes are clearly reported. The lack of CCND3 changes (C134) provides an important internal control. These are among the most upregulated genes in MTF2∆ cells (C130), supporting their functional importance.

results.result: All three D-type cyclin promoters contain CpG islands, but CCND1 and CCND2 have regions ~7× larger (7460 and 6003 bp) than CCND3 (996 bp). CCND1 contains ~2× more CpG repeats than CCND2 (575 vs 379) and ~6× more than CCND3 (575 vs 95), suggesting CpG island-dependent regulation of CCND1/CCND2 but not CCND3 by MTF2.
results.evaluation: The quantitative analysis of CpG island size and density (C135-C138) provides a mechanistic explanation for differential MTF2 regulation. The correlation between CpG island size/density and MTF2-dependent regulation (C139) is consistent with PCL proteins' known CpG island-binding properties. This elegantly explains the selective regulation of CCND1/CCND2.

results.result: Western blotting showed increased CCND1 and CCND2 (but not CCND3) protein levels in pooled knockouts of MTF2, EZH2, EED, and SUZ12, but not JARID2. Clonal SUZ12∆ and MTF2∆ (but not JARID2∆) lines showed increased mRNA and protein for CCND1/CCND2 but not CCND3.
results.evaluation: The protein-level validation (C140-C142) confirms the RNA-Seq results and demonstrates functional consequences. Testing both pooled and clonal knockouts strengthens confidence. The consistent pattern across core PRC2 and MTF2 but not JARID2 supports the PRC2.1-specific effect. The lack of CCND3 changes provides an important negative control.

results.result: None of the E-type cyclins, CIP/KIP CDK inhibitors, RB1, or E2F proteins displayed significantly altered mRNA transcript abundance in MTF2∆ or JARID2∆ lines.
results.evaluation: This negative result (C143) is important for demonstrating specificity. The lack of changes in other canonical G1/S regulators suggests CCND1/CCND2 are the primary PRC2.1 targets affecting palbociclib sensitivity. Western blot confirmation of protein levels strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: GSK126 treatment (6 days) reduced H3K27me3 levels in all cell lines tested and increased CCND1 expression in HAP1, KBM7, MDA-MB-231, and COS7 cells, but not in LNCaP or NR-6 cells, demonstrating context-dependent regulation.
results.evaluation: The panel of cell lines (C144-C149) demonstrates that PRC2 regulation of CCND1 occurs in multiple contexts (CML, breast cancer, immortalized cells) but not universally. The inclusion of KBM7 (HAP1 parent line, C146) rules out HAP1-specific artifacts. The context-dependence (C149) is consistent with known PRC2 biology and appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Depletion of SUZ12 or MTF2 in COS7 and MDA-MB-231 cells resulted in significantly increased CCND1 expression, confirming that MTF2-containing PRC2.1 represses CCND1 in diverse cell types beyond HAP1.
results.evaluation: The genetic validation in additional cell lines (C150) confirms the pharmacological results and demonstrates the effect is not HAP1-specific. Testing both a breast cancer line and immortalized fibroblasts strengthens generalizability. This addresses a key concern about context-dependence.

results.result: Overexpression of CCND1 or CCND2 was sufficient to induce palbociclib resistance. Increased association of CCND1 with FLAG-tagged CDK6 was observed in SUZ12∆ and MTF2∆ (but not JARID2∆) cells, suggesting elevated D-type cyclins drive formation of active CDK4/6 complexes.
results.evaluation: The overexpression experiment (C151) demonstrates sufficiency of CCND1/CCND2 for palbociclib resistance. The co-IP data (C152) shows increased CCND1-CDK6 association in PRC2.1 mutants, supporting increased complex formation. Together, these establish a causal link between PRC2.1 loss, cyclin upregulation, and palbociclib resistance.

results.result: MTF2∆ cells maintained a higher ratio of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated RB1 at each palbociclib concentration tested compared to WT or JARID2∆ cells. This suggests increased CCND1/CCND2 levels in MTF2∆ cells increase CDK4/6 kinase activity, driving S-phase entry.
results.evaluation: The RB1 phosphorylation data (C153) directly demonstrate increased CDK4/6 activity in MTF2∆ cells despite palbociclib treatment. Combined with the BrdU incorporation data (C99) showing increased S-phase entry, this establishes the mechanistic link (C154) between cyclin upregulation and palbociclib resistance through the canonical CDK4/6-RB1 pathway.

results.result: MTF2-containing PRC2.1 antagonizes G1 progression by repressing expression of D-type cyclins CCND1 and CCND2 in certain cellular contexts.
results.evaluation: This main conclusion (C155) is well-supported by the comprehensive data: (1) genetic screens identify PRC2.1 as palbociclib resistance factor, (2) MTF2∆ cells show loss of H3K27me3 at CCND1/CCND2 promoters, (3) CCND1/CCND2 are upregulated in MTF2∆ cells, (4) this leads to increased CDK4/6 activity and S-phase entry, (5) the effect is validated in multiple cell types. The caveat about context-dependence is appropriate.

results.result: The authors performed a CRISPR-Cas9 whole-genome screen using the Toronto Knockout Library in HAP1 cells to identify genes that alter sensitivity to three cell cycle inhibitors (camptothecin, colchicine, and palbociclib). The screen used 70,948 guides targeting 18,053 protein-coding genes, with cells propagated for 18 days in drug or DMSO, and genes were considered significant if they met specific statistical thresholds (differential effect ±0.5, FDR <0.4).
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the screen as well-designed and executed. One reviewer states 'The strengths of the paper are the design and execution of the chemogenetic screen, which provides a wealth of potentially useful information.' Another notes 'The initial CRISPR screen is very interesting...This screen mostly identified known cell cycle regulators, which demonstrates the validity of the approach.' The methodology is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: The camptothecin and colchicine screens identified expected hits (DNA damage repair genes for camptothecin, mitotic spindle genes for colchicine) as well as unexpected pathways. The screens showed drug-specific effects with little overlap between conditions (only 13 and 20 genes showed non-specific sensitivity or resistance across all compounds).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge these results exist and provide useful information, one reviewer explicitly notes a weakness: 'the results from the colchicine and camptothecin screens (Fig. 1 and 2) are not experimentally validated, which lessens the rigor of those data and conclusions.' The lack of validation creates uncertainty about these findings despite their internal consistency.

results.result: The palbociclib screen identified expected G1/S regulators including CCNE1 (2nd most important), CDK6 (24th), CDK2 (27th), CCND2 (29th), and CCND1 (46th) as important for palbociclib sensitivity, while RB1 mutation conferred substantial resistance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as validation of the screen's ability to identify known biology. One reviewer notes 'This screen mostly identified known cell cycle regulators, which demonstrates the validity of the approach.' The identification of expected hits is treated as evidence supporting the screen's quality rather than being questioned.

results.result: The palbociclib screen revealed sensitivity in cells with sgRNAs targeting H4 acetylation, positive regulators of Pol II transcription, and DDR regulators, consistent with long-term palbociclib treatment inducing DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. The interpretation about DNA damage is supported by citations to recent publications, and no reviewer questions this aspect of the results. The findings are treated as part of the broader characterization of palbociclib effects.

results.result: Almost 25% of genes conferring unique resistance to palbociclib are associated with mitochondrial function, and combined treatment with mitochondrial inhibitors (rotenone, TTFA, oligomycin) and palbociclib showed positive proliferation interactions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these mitochondrial findings. The data showing dose-dependent interactions between mitochondrial inhibitors and palbociclib (Figure 3D and supplements) are presented with quantitative results and statistical analysis that reviewers do not challenge.

results.result: Mutation of PRC2 core components (EZH2, SUZ12, EED) resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib (ranking 8th, 4th, and 3rd strongest hits out of 18,053 genes), but not to camptothecin or colchicine. PRC1 components also showed resistance, while H2AK119ub1 deubiquitinase complex members showed sensitivity.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept this as a major finding. The editor states 'Convincing evidence is provided that resistance to palbociclib can result from loss of PRC2.1 activity.' Another reviewer notes 'The most interesting outcome of the experiment is the finding that knockouts of the PRC2.1 complex make the cell resistant to Palbociclib.' The specificity to palbociclib and not other drugs strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Pharmacological inhibition of EZH2 with GSK126 resulted in cells withstanding palbociclib-induced proliferation suppression after 9 days of treatment.
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically critiques this result: 'conclusions drawn from data in Fig. 4D are not fully supported by proper use of biological replicates and analysis of the results.' In revision comments, the reviewer states 'Proper statistical analysis considering biological replicates is still not applied to determine whether differences in palbociclib IC50 values at different GSK126 concentrations are significant.' This indicates the evidence is insufficient.

results.result: PRC2.1 components (MTF2, PHF1, PHF19, EPOP) conferred resistance to palbociclib, with MTF2 being the strongest, while PRC2.2 components (JARID2, AEBP2) showed neutral or enhanced sensitivity. Validation experiments with sgRNA pools confirmed these differential effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently accept the differential roles of PRC2.1 vs PRC2.2. One states 'The data convincingly demonstrate in the HAP1 cell line that the MTF2-PRC2 complex sustains the effects of palbociclib.' Another notes 'they confirmed that MTF2 is particularly important to repress the cyclins CCND1 and CCND2.' The validation experiments are not questioned.

results.result: Monoclonal knockout cell lines showed that MTF2Δ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib (IC50 increased ~2.6-fold), with more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib, while JARID2Δ cells were slightly more sensitive. No increase in apoptosis markers was detected.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these validation experiments in clonal lines. One reviewer notes 'The data convincingly demonstrate in the HAP1 cell line that the MTF2-PRC2 complex sustains the effects of palbociclib (Fig. 4).' The BrdU incorporation and apoptosis data are not challenged, supporting the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Western blotting showed no change in bulk H3K27me3 levels in MTF2Δ and JARID2Δ cells, while SUZ12Δ cells displayed a significant reduction (p=0.0104), suggesting phenotypic changes are due to altered localization rather than overall abundance of the mark.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these western blot results. The finding that MTF2 and JARID2 deletion don't affect bulk levels but do affect localization is consistent with the subsequent CUT&RUN data showing locus-specific changes, which reviewers accept.

results.result: CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq analysis revealed that MTF2Δ cells showed significantly more promoters with decreased H3K27me3 (5808 vs 1034 in JARID2Δ) and more upregulated transcripts (733 vs 114), with most being MTF2-specific. PCA showed no large differences in H3K27me3 distribution with palbociclib treatment, suggesting MTF2 affects basal gene expression rather than drug-induced adaptation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these genome-wide profiling results. One states 'The data convincingly demonstrate in the HAP1 cell line that the MTF2-PRC2 complex...methylates H3K27 in CpG-rich promoters (Fig. 5).' The comprehensive nature of the analysis and the clear differential effects between MTF2 and JARID2 are not questioned.

results.result: MTF2Δ cells showed complete loss of H3K27me3 at CpG islands genome-wide (Fisher's exact test, OR=20.4, p=2.2×10⁻³⁰⁸), while JARID2Δ showed only partial loss (OR=9.8, p=6.5×10⁻⁷). This indicates PRC2.1 is required for all H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands, while PRC2.2 is only required for achieving full wild-type levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings about differential roles at CpG islands. One reviewer notes the study 'methylates H3K27 in CpG-rich promoters (Fig. 5)' without questioning the data. The statistical analysis is robust and the interpretation about PRC2.1 vs PRC2.2 roles is consistent with the broader dataset.

results.result: CCND1 and CCND2 promoters lost H3K27me3 signal and showed strong transcriptional induction in MTF2Δ cells (4.3 and 2.7 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3, respectively), but not in JARID2Δ cells. CCND1 and CCND2 have larger CpG islands (~7× larger than CCND3) and more CpG repeats, explaining their MTF2-dependent regulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently accept this as the key mechanistic finding. One states 'they confirmed that MTF2 is particularly important to repress the cyclins CCND1 and CCND2. Absence of MTF2 therefore leads to increased expression of these genes, sufficient to make the cell resistant to Palbociclib.' The CpG island analysis explaining specificity is not questioned.

results.result: Western blot validation in pooled and clonal knockouts confirmed increased CCND1 and CCND2 protein levels in MTF2Δ, EZH2Δ, EED Δ, and SUZ12Δ cells, but not JARID2Δ or CCND3. Other cell cycle regulators (E-type cyclins, CIP/KIP inhibitors, RB1, E2F proteins) showed no significant changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these validation experiments. One notes 'The data convincingly demonstrate in the HAP1 cell line that the MTF2-PRC2 complex...represses Cyclin D expression (Fig. 6).' The specificity to CCND1/2 and not other cell cycle genes strengthens the mechanistic model.

results.result: GSK126 treatment increased CCND1 levels in HAP1, KBM7, MDA-MB-231, and COS7 cells, but not in LNCaP or NR-6 cells. Genetic depletion of SUZ12 and MTF2 in COS7 and MDA-MB-231 also increased CCND1, demonstrating PRC2.1's role in repressing CCND1 across multiple cell lineages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the demonstration of effects across multiple cell lines. The editor notes 'The effect of PRC2.1 on cyclin D is not universal across tested cell lines with the causal differences not yet understood,' acknowledging both the positive results in some lines and the context-dependence. One reviewer notes 'The work is limited to specific biological contexts, and the generality of the conclusions is uncertain,' but this is about scope rather than validity of the data shown.

results.result: Overexpression of CCND1 or CCND2 was sufficient to induce palbociclib resistance. MTF2Δ and SUZ12Δ cells showed increased CCND1-CDK6 association and maintained higher phosphorylated/unphosphorylated RB1 ratios at all palbociclib concentrations, indicating increased CDK4/6 activity drives cells into S-phase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this mechanistic conclusion linking cyclin D upregulation to resistance. One states 'The study shows that increased expression of D-type cyclins results in palbociclib resistance.' The co-IP and RB1 phosphorylation data provide direct mechanistic evidence that reviewers do not challenge.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on screen methodology (C1, C2, C46-C49). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED and acknowledge the screen as well-designed with appropriate coverage, statistical thresholds, and validation through expected hits.

Complete agreement on CDK4/6-RB1-E2F pathway validation (C56-C61). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, recognizing recovery of canonical pathway components as validation of screen quality and identification of known cell cycle regulators.

Agreement on DDR gene sensitivity findings (C73-C75). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the interpretation that palbociclib induces DNA damage and the role of chromatin-modifying complexes.
Agreement on mitochondrial gene enrichment (C76-C77). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the pharmacological validation and dose-dependent effects without challenge.

Disagreement on EZH2 inhibitor validation (C87). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on dose-response data, but peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, specifically critiquing lack of proper biological replicates and statistical analysis of IC50 differences.

Agreement on bulk H3K27me3 findings (C102-C103). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the differential effects between MTF2/JARID2 deletions versus SUZ12 deletion as mechanistically informative.

Strong agreement on PRC2 resistance findings (C78-C86). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED and recognize this as a major finding. Peer review emphasizes this as the most interesting outcome, with convincing evidence for PRC2.1 specificity.

Agreement on protein-level validation of CCND1/CCND2 upregulation (C140-C142). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the validation across pooled and clonal knockouts with appropriate negative controls.

Agreement on differential PRC2.1/PRC2.2 roles at CpG islands (C121-C126). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the statistical analysis showing MTF2 requirement for H3K27me3 at CpG islands with highly significant p-values.

Agreement on context-dependence across cell lines (C144-C149). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, acknowledging that PRC2 regulation of CCND1 occurs in multiple contexts but not universally, with appropriate recognition of limitations.

Agreement on genome-wide CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq analysis (C104-C118). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the comprehensive profiling showing MTF2 affects more genes than JARID2 and that H3K27me3 distribution changes are independent of palbociclib treatment.

Agreement on differential PRC2.1 vs PRC2.2 effects (C88-C91, with peer also covering C92-C93). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting MTF2 as particularly important and the opposing effects of the two subcomplexes as a key finding.

Strong agreement on CCND1/CCND2 as key MTF2 targets (C129-C134, with peer also covering C135-C139). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED and recognize this as the central mechanistic finding linking MTF2 to palbociclib resistance.

Agreement on overexpression and co-IP experiments (C151-C152, with peer also covering C153-C155). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the demonstration of sufficiency and increased CCND1-CDK6 association as causal evidence.

Agreement on RB1 phosphorylation mechanism (C153-C154, with peer also covering C151-C152, C155). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the direct demonstration of increased CDK4/6 activity and mechanistic link through canonical pathway.

Agreement on CpG island size/density analysis (C135-C139, with peer also covering C129-C134). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanistic explanation for selective CCND1/CCND2 regulation based on CpG island properties.

Agreement on IC50 validation with multiple CDK4/6 inhibitors (C96-C98, with peer also covering C94-C95, C99-C101). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the quantitative measurements and demonstration that effects are not palbociclib-specific.

Agreement on BrdU incorporation and apoptosis data (C99-C101, with peer also covering C94-C98). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting that PRC2.1 loss allows cell cycle progression despite palbociclib without differential cell death.

Partial disagreement on camptothecin screen results (C50-C55). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on recovery of known targets and internal consistency. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting lack of experimental validation lessens rigor despite acknowledging the data provides useful information.

Partial disagreement on colchicine screen results (C53, C69-C72). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on mechanistic consistency. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN for broader colchicine/camptothecin results (C50-C72), citing lack of experimental validation.

Agreement on PCA and DESeq2 genome-wide analysis (C104-C108, with peer also covering C109-C118). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting that H3K27me3 distribution doesn't change with palbociclib while transcripts do, supporting basal gene expression effects.

Agreement on specificity of CCND1/CCND2 regulation (C143). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the negative result for other G1/S regulators as demonstrating specificity and strengthening the mechanistic model.

Disagreement on chromatin/RNA metabolism resistance interpretation (C65-C68). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting unexpected findings and speculative KICSTOR-mTOR-RNF168 mechanism. Peer review rates broader camptothecin results as UNCERTAIN but for different reason (lack of validation rather than mechanistic speculation).

Agreement on competitive proliferation assays (C92-C93, with peer also covering C88-C91). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the validation with independent methodology and appropriate statistical analysis.

Agreement on rationale for focusing on MTF2 and SUZ12 (C94-C95, with peer also covering C96-C101). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the justification based on literature and avoiding compensation effects.

Agreement on protein-coding gene enrichment (C119-C120, with peer also covering C121-C128). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting this observation as important for interpreting functional consequences and focusing pathway analysis.

Agreement on CpG island prevalence and pathway analysis (C127-C128, with peer also covering C119-C126). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanistic link between MTF2's CpG island targeting and G1 regulation through cell cycle gene enrichment.

Agreement on main conclusion (C155, with peer also covering C151-C154). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the comprehensive mechanistic model linking PRC2.1 loss to CCND1/CCND2 upregulation to palbociclib resistance, with appropriate caveats about context-dependence.

Disagreement on specificity of hits to individual inhibitors (C62-C64). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing this demonstrates biologically relevant phase-specific regulators. Peer review rates broader results as UNCERTAIN due to lack of experimental validation for colchicine/camptothecin screens.

Agreement on genetic validation in additional cell lines (C150, with peer also covering C144-C149). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the confirmation in breast cancer and immortalized fibroblast lines as demonstrating the effect is not HAP1-specific.
